title: Platonic Representations in the Human Brain: Unsupervised Recovery of Universal Geometry
claim: A three-stage procedure learns per-subject embeddings, aligns them pairwise by rotation, then synchronizes them into one shared space.
layout: 3 panels (A top, B and C bottom), left-to-right, blob-shaped latent spaces
description: Panel A spans the top. Sampled images and a brain icon feed an fMRI response vector X into a blue rounded box labeled 'Subject encoder f_s'. Inside, colored-cell vectors pass through reliability scaling, PCA and MCCA, grouped as a 'Linear projection' bracket. They then enter a small neural network with a skip connection weighted by α, labeled 'Nonlinear refinement'. The output is a green blob, the subject latent space Z^(s). Panel B (bottom left) shows two encoders f_s and f_t, drawn as blue trapezoids, each producing a green blob. Curved arrows labeled R_{s→t} and R_{t→s} connect the blobs. Panel C (bottom right) shows a central green circle Z connected by paired arrows to several subject blobs Z^(1), Z^(s) and Z^(S). The arrows are labeled R_1, R_1^T, R_S and R_S^T. Green and blue are the main colors, with orange and blue cells in the vectors.
caption: Method overview. (A) Subject encoder. For each subject, fMRI responses are mapped into a low-dimensional embedding space using voxel reliability weighting, PCA, and multi-view CCA (MCCA), followed by a residual nonlinear refinement trained from repeated stimulus presentations. (B) Pairwise brain-to-brain translation. Independently learned subject embeddings are translated between subject pairs by estimating orthogonal rotations Rs→t from geometry-derived pseudocorrespondences. (C) Shared latent space. Pairwise rotations are synchronized to recover one orthogonal transformation Rs per subject, mapping all subject embeddings into a common space.
abstract: The Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that representational convergence in artificial neural networks can be harnessed constructively: embeddings can be translated across models through a universal latent space without paired data. We ask whether an analogous geometry can be recovered across human brains. Using fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we propose a self-supervised encoder that learns subject-specific embeddings from brain data alone by exploiting repeated stimulus presentations. We show that these independently learned spaces can be translated across subjects using unsupervised orthogonal rotations, without paired cross-subject samples or intermediate model representations. Synchronizing pairwise rotations into a single shared latent space further improves cross-subject retrieval. These results provide evidence for a shared geometry in learned representations of human visual responses: subject-specific fMRI embeddings can be aligned across individuals within a common coordinate system.
